full_text:
Persistent drought conditions caused by the climate crisis are expected to cause further disruption to trains across England, as the lack of rainfall affects the ground supporting railway embankments.
On Tuesday, South Western Railway (SWR) became the latest large rail company to announce timetable changes and reduced speeds to cope with the effects of hot and dry weather.
From Monday 10 August, trains between Yeovil and Exeter St Davids will be reduced to one every two hours, under an amended timetable. Passengers travelling between London Waterloo and Exeter are also advised to allow extra time to complete their journeys, which are expected to take up to 27 minutes longer. Full details of the expected disruption have been published on the company’s website.
The move comes after operators in the east of England said they were going to take similar steps. Network Rail said last week that late-night speed restrictions and altered timetables would need to come into effect from 3 August “until the ground conditions have recovered”.
Affected routes include those run by Great Northern in Cambridgeshire and Norfolk, by Greater Anglia and c2c in Essex, and the eastern end of the Elizabeth line from London.
The moves are in response to “soil moisture deficit” (SMD) caused by spring’s unusually low rainfall followed by hot, dry summer weather as the UK enters its fourth heatwave of the year.
Many sections of Britain’s railway network are built on embankments containing clay soil, which normally contains a lot of water. Long periods of drought reduce the volume of moisture in the soil, causing it to shrink, which in turn disturbs the ground that tracks are built on, causing sleepers to drop or move out of position.
Even relatively small changes in track geometry – the positioning, alignment and measurements of the line – mean trains must reduce their speed to run safely.
SWR’s West of England line is particularly vulnerable to the problem of SMD, with the rail operator taking similar steps a year ago after another dry spring and summer.
Lawrence Bowman, the managing director of SWR and Network Rail Wessex, said: “Extreme weather events are becoming increasingly common, and this is the second year in a row that prolonged hot, dry weather has affected our network.
“Since last summer’s intervention, we’ve invested in strengthening the route, carried out extensive work to the track and embankments, and developed a plan that customers can rely on.
“As a result of that careful planning, we’ve managed to reduce journey times in our amended timetable by around 30 minutes compared to last year, minimising the impact on our customers while also keeping them safe.”
Last week, Great Northern announced timetable changes from 3 August on the Great Northern line to and from King’s Lynn in Norfolk. Greater Anglia will alter some evening Essex services including rail replacement buses, some late c2c services to Shoeburyness will change, and the Elizabeth line will operate a reduced 11pm to midnight service between Gidea Park and Shenfield on certain dates.
Network Rail said its engineers reduce the effects of dried-out soil by using machines called tampers to lift the track, push stone ballast underneath and create a solid foundation so trains can run smoothly. New ballast is also put down to help raise the level of the track.
Last year, engineers treated about 62 miles (100km) of track on Anglia routes using tampers to help tackle the effects of dried-out soil. In the run-up to summer, teams have already dropped thousands of tonnes of ballast to help keep the track as smooth as possible, with 49,000 tonnes expected to be used over the course of 2026.

'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires
For the past week, firefighters have been tackling a series of wildfires ravaging the Spanish countryside, threatening dozens of communities and forcing tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes.
Three fires in the Madrid region have caused particular concern, with a new heatwave expected to hit Spain from Wednesday, fuelling fears that firefighting efforts could be hindered.
"It's a hell of a situation," said Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, as she visited affected areas on Monday alongside Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
Sánchez spoke on Tuesday of highly challenging hours and days ahead, but of light beginning to appear "at the end of the tunnel".
Temperatures are expected to approach 40C in some regions in the coming days, with the heatwave forecast to last at least until Sunday.
Spain's state meteorological agency Aemet has warned the "fire danger level will continue to rise to extreme levels, hindering firefighting efforts".
Regional authorities began lifting some evacuation and lockdown orders on Tuesday as conditions improved - including in parts of the Madrid region - but restrictions remain in place in the worst-affected areas.
In the Madrid region alone, more than 56,500 people have been evacuated since the fires broke out last week. A further 27,797 people have been ordered to stay at home.
Further evacuations have taken place in Ávila, Toledo and Valencia.
Ayuso had earlier described the wildfires as "the biggest natural catastrophe in the history of Spain".
She wrote on X that the situation was now "improving little by little" and some residents may soon be allowed to return home.
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spain's La 1 TV channel that firefighting efforts on Monday night had resulted in "relatively positive progress".
"This morning, we are very satisfied with the work done. We are going to consolidate the work that has been done," he said.
He maintained that "we must be positive; we have the emergency under control" but conceded that "weather conditions are not helping us at all".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on Tuesday that areas affected by the wildfires have been declared "disaster zones".
"The climate emergency is worsening year after year, and we are required to be united to fight against fire, as well as in prevention and reconstruction," he told reporters during a briefing in Madrid.
"Therefore, I make an explicit request, a single appeal to all regional governments: Climate denial is the worst fuel for the fight against the climate emergency."
Spanish journalist Juan Navarro, who is in Cebreros - a town around 40 miles west of Madrid – told the BBC that people were looking with fear to the next heatwave.
When you drive through villages in the area around Cebreros, "everything is black", he said.
The mayors of two of the evacuated towns in the Madrid region described the fire as "a kitten by night and a lion by day".
Robledo de Chavela mayor Fernando Casado said his community would continue fighting "with their knives out".
Echoing his sentiments, Valdemaqueda mayor Ricardo Meneses added that "we can't let our guard down and we're on high alert because now is the time to stop the fire".
A psychologist visiting shelters has told El Mundo there is a growing sense of anxiety among the evacuees.
"We've seen cases of people who come in relatively relaxed on the first day because they think this situation might only last a day," said Sara Casado, of the Citizen Services Department of the Madrid region.
"But then they see how the hours and days go by. That uncertainty of being here without knowing when they'll be able to return increases their anxiety."
The Madrid region is currently under a red weather warning, with temperatures expected to reach 35C in mountainous areas and 38C in other parts of the community.
In its latest update, the national government's delegation in Madrid said the fire "remains active and uncontrolled".
"Today's efforts will focus on surveillance and cooling the affected areas in anticipation of the forecast worsening of weather conditions," it added.
Around 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) have been affected by the fires in Spain, according to the minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen.
The wildfire burning in the Ávila area was the largest in the country's recent history, she added.
In Ávila, where more than 50,000 hectares have burned down since the start of the wildfires, the government's representative said the fire had a "quite favourable" evolution overnight.
Nicanor Sen, however, said there had been "small flare-ups" that were now being monitored by emergency services.
Meanwhile, the government of Valencia lifted a lockdown order for the town of Vall D'Uixo after a fire broke out of 25 July, forcing some 16,000 from 20 municipalities to evacuate.
However, the local council's fire department representative, David Vicente, told the press on Tuesday afternoon that the fire remains "very active".
In neighbouring Portugal, firefighters are tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area.
The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (Ipma) has put large parts of the country under a very high red fire alert, with some areas under the highest warning level.

search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
Fact checked by Nick Blackmer
Hot weather puts extra stress on your body during exercise and raises the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke.
Exercise earlier or later in the day, stay hydrated, and ease into workouts as temperatures rise.
Stop exercising immediately if you develop symptoms of heat illness and seek emergency care if you suspect heat stroke.
Warm, sunny days can jump-start your workouts and make them feel more appealing, but heat changes how your body responds to exercise. When temperatures climb, your heart works harder, you sweat more, and your body has to work to keep your core temperature within a safe range. So while your muscles and nervous system might be more primed, higher temperatures can increase the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion, and, in severe cases, heat stroke.
That being said, you don’t have to skip exercise altogether. With the right timing, pacing, hydration, and warning-sign awareness, you can stay active more safely when it’s hot outside.
1. Exercise During Cooler Hours
The simplest heat-safety strategy is timing. The CDC recommends limiting outdoor activity during the middle of the day, when the sun is hottest, and scheduling workouts earlier or later when possible.
Try exercising:
Early in the morning
Near sunset
In shaded areas
Indoors, if needed, especially during heat advisories
Even if the air temperature seems manageable, pavement, turf, and direct sunlight can make conditions feel much hotter. On especially hot or humid days, consider swapping out outdoor workouts for swimming, indoor cycling, or strength training.
2. Ease Into Heat Exposure
Your body can absolutely adapt to exercising in heat, but it takes time. Heat acclimatization means gradually exposing yourself to warmer conditions so your body becomes more efficient at sweating, regulating temperature, and maintaining blood volume.
Consensus recommendations suggest repeated exercise-heat exposures over one to two weeks. That doesn’t mean you should jump into intense workouts right away. Start with shorter, easier sessions and slowly increase duration or intensity.
Here are some tips:
Cut your usual workout time or intensity for the first few hot days
Take more breaks than usual
Add time gradually (slower is better) over one to two weeks
3. Drink Fluids Before, During, and After Exercise
Hydration helps your body sweat and maintain circulation. It’s no surprise that on hot days, the CDC advises drinking more water than usual and not waiting until you feel thirsty. Even better is to pre-hydrate so you’re already starting from an optimal position. Then, during your session, drink as needed, and afterward, make sure you’re also taking in enough fluids.
For most moderate workouts, water is enough. But for longer sessions, especially in the heat and when you’re sweating heavily, electrolyte-rich beverages help replace sodium lost through sweating.

title: SpaceX Has Nosedived 50% From Its All-Time High, and It May Realistically Lose Another 50% Before Its Valuation Makes Any Sense - The Motley Fool

full_text:
On June 12, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence (AI) and space infrastructure conglomerate rewrote Wall Street's record books. Including the underwriters' overallotment, Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) (SPCX +2.56%) raised $85.7 billion and vaulted to a valuation of nearly $3 trillion just days after its initial public offering (IPO).
But this initial buzz has quickly faded. Since peaking at $225.64 per share on June 16, SpaceX shares have plunged roughly 50% to $113.37 (its after-hours closing price on July 24).
Statistically, the average year-one max drawdown in technology-driven IPOs over the last 14 years is 55%, according to data from Truist Financial. Thus far, SpaceX is par for the course. However, history suggests that things may get considerably worse before they have any chance of turning around.
SpaceX's IPO-mania has faded away
Aside from the buzz of going public, SpaceX's stock was initially driven by newly amended rules that allowed for its early inclusion in the Nasdaq-100, Russell 1000, and Russell 3000. Investors piled in with the expectation that passive/index funds would spend tens of billions of dollars purchasing SpaceX shares.
Unfortunately, reality is beginning to set in. Musk's trillion-dollar AI and space giant is set to report its quarterly operating results on Aug. 4. While AI start-up xAI has landed a few notable compute deals, SpaceX isn't particularly close to recurring profits, nor has it yet established that its operations are sustainable.
Great look at the SpaceX shares unlock schedule as well as the potential passive buying schedule from @JSeyff @FrancisSharoon Depending on the early post-IPO returns, this could really play with and disperse the returns of "passive" funds (which is why there's arguably no such... pic.twitter.com/KOuEkJlngF
-- Eric Balchunas (@EricBalchunas) May 28, 2026
Additionally, some early release-eligible insiders (high-ranking executives, board members, and early investors) can begin selling some of their shares two trading days after SpaceX reports its quarterly results. SpaceX's accelerated and staggered share unlock schedule may be nothing more than a massive wealth transfer from retail investors to insiders.
Valuation concerns are also clearly in the picture. Even after a 50% drawdown from its all-time high, SpaceX is trading at an estimated 38 times forecast sales this year. No company at the forefront of any game-changing trend (let alone two: AI and the space economy) has ever sustained a price-to-sales ratio above 30 for any considerable period.
Historical precedent suggests SpaceX can lose another 50%
However, history might just be the most glaring issue for SpaceX.
Although AI is the hottest technological trend since the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s, we've witnessed every next-big-thing technology for more than three decades navigate a bubble-bursting event. This is to say that investors have persistently overshot the adoption and/or optimization timeline of every game-changing technology for decades -- and there's no reason to believe AI is an exception.
Stock market bubbles throughout history...

AI stocks now ~40% of the market. pic.twitter.com/RxSAh09k6F
SpaceX securing significant compute deals from Alphabet and Anthropic demonstrates that AI doesn't have an adoption issue. But we're likely several years away from businesses optimizing AI solutions to boost their sales and profits. It took until after the dot-com bubble burst before internet-driven companies understood how to maximize this technology, and AI is likely on a similar path.
According to SpaceX's prospectus, xAI represents 93% of its estimated $28.5 trillion addressable market. If the AI bubble bursts, as history suggests it will, SpaceX will have little in the way of a foundation to fall back on.
Based on history, SpaceX could realistically lose another 50% before its valuation even comes close to making sense.

Recorded rainfall

Waterlogged roads, flooded markets, and slow-moving traffic disrupted life in Delhi on Tuesday morning as heavy showers battered the city, prompting the weather office to issue a red alert for thunderstorms, lightning, and rain over the next few hours.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast a generally cloudy sky with heavy rainfall for the rest of the day, warning of thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and intense spells of rain across the national capital.

Happy Tuesday, everyone!
A Heat Advisory remains in effect until 9 pm tonight.
Please take frequent breaks if you have to be outside for a prolonged period of time and drink plenty of fluids.
This afternoon, highs are expected to be around 100 degrees with a heat index of 110 to 115 degrees.
Overnight, it will be warm and humid with lows in the upper 70s.
Wednesday will be a repeat of today with highs near 100 and a heat index of 110 to 115 degrees.
Rain chances will be much better, which will lower our highs down into the mid-90s on Thursday and the lower 90s for the weekend.
Lows will be in the lower 70s.
